A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MOA and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Shared content can be matched reliably across the reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original MOA training and evaluation on PersonaGym and RoleMRC, including model and component ablations in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds baseline comparisons, general-capability evaluations, and mechanism and robustness analyses.

M1.justification: Algorithm 2 corrects its bookkeeping: the LIS list stores pairs (x, y), rather than scalar y values, and binary search explicitly uses the last coordinate. The core pivot selection, reward weighting, objective, and rollout strategy remain unchanged. This is a pseudocode correction; the PDFs do not establish a corresponding experimental rerun.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on MMLU, MMLU-Pro, HellaSwag, and GSM8K in Appendix F, extending coverage from role-playing to general knowledge, commonsense completion, and mathematical reasoning. The original RoleMRC/OpenCharacter training coverage and PersonaGym/RoleMRC evaluations remain.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds evaluated CharacterLLM, CharacterGLM, and DPO baselines. RLOO and MOA (RLOO), previously evaluated in v1, disappear rather than moving to an appendix. MOA (GRPO) is renamed MOA; GPT-4o, Claude-3.7, SFT, and GRPO remain.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include Claude scoring of PersonaGym, a pipeline using Qwen3-Max for rewards and off-policy generation, checkpoint-based Pareto analysis, and DPO preferences constructed from GPT-4o versus SFT responses. These substantially expand the experimental controls. The original splits, model configurations, decoding settings, and training budgets are retained in Appendix B.

E4.justification: Appendices E–K add single-reward training ablations, Pareto-front analysis, out-of-domain tests, conflict-filter inspection and removal ablation, alternative evaluator and reward-generator checks, and runtime analysis. Two qualitative SFT/MOA cases are also added. These substantially expand investigation of mechanisms and robustness, although the RLOO transfer experiment is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report averaging three evaluations per PersonaGym question; this moves from Section 4.1 to Appendix B. No new seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, or statistical uncertainty estimation is reported. The additional judge comparisons test robustness rather than sampling uncertainty.

E6.justification: Matched MOA results remain unchanged, including Qwen3-8B averages of 4.75 on PersonaGym and 0.75 on RoleMRC. However, v2 adds substantial new results and removes the RLOO entries. New findings include RoleMRC averages of 0.56 without conflict elimination versus 0.58 with it, and mixed general-capability results in Figure 7. These are newly reported comparisons, not cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The existing mathematical definitions, theorems, assumptions, and Appendix A proofs are unchanged. Appendix J adds a limited analytical cost argument: precomputing one of G rollouts gives an approximate GRPO/MOA runtime ratio of G/(G−1), evaluated as 16/15.

C1.justification: The main MOA contribution and claimed 21% RoleMRC improvement over GPT-4o remain. The introduction narrows superiority from all metrics to most metrics, while the contribution list replaces the standalone diversified-rollout contribution with emphasis on pivot-based weighting. The abstract also qualifies closed-model competitiveness by evaluation protocol.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations connecting individual rewards to evaluation dimensions, explaining filtering trade-offs and runtime, and arguing evaluator robustness and general-capability retention. New case discussions attribute SFT behavior to superficial style imitation. Some interpretations overreach: Figure 7 shows a substantial MMLU decrease despite the broad retention claim. Section 6's original limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 newly discloses off-policy sample precomputation, DPO preference construction, and per-step training times of 1.95 minutes for GRPO and 1.83 for MOA. Existing hardware, learning rates, sampling parameters, and training budgets are relocated essentially intact to Appendix B.

R1.justification: Section 2 refocuses the reasoning discussion on role-playing RL, adds COMEDY, and sharpens the comparison with MOPO. CharacterGLM, general-capability benchmarks, robustness, and memory research receive additional citations; RLOO, CPPO, and Absolute Zero references are removed. The fundamental positioning remains multi-objective rubric-based training for role-playing agents.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial method and results prose are rewritten. Training and benchmark descriptions move into dedicated appendices, the contribution list is recast, and an appendix contents guide is added. This substantially changes the narrative and organization.

P2.justification: v2 adds qualitative comparison Figures 5 and 8, Pareto Figure 6, general-capability Figure 7, and Tables 6–10. Table 1's comparison structure changes, and several existing displays are relocated or reformatted. The original reward-prompt figures are preserved as Figures 9–11.

improvement.justification: The single-reward and conflict-elimination ablations and alternative-judge checks provide useful validation absent from v1, while the reorganization improves navigation. These gains are moderated by lost RLOO coverage and overinterpretation of some additions: Figure 7 reports MMLU scores of 54.0 for SFT and 42.9 for MOA despite claiming general-capability retention. The evidence supports a limited net improvement.
